column5: What does fd replace and what is its key advantage?
column6: fd replaces find. Key advantages: respects .gitignore by default, regex patterns, colorized output, simpler syntax. Example: fd -e yaml finds all YAML files vs find . -name '*.yaml' -type f\n\nRemember: fd = modern find. Smart case, colorized, .gitignore-aware. Simpler syntax.

column5: How do you find and execute a command on matching files with fd?
column6: fd -e py -x wc -l (count lines in each Python file). fd -e log -X rm (delete all .log files — -X batches into one command, -x runs per file). Add -H to include hidden files.\n\nRemember: fd = modern find. Smart case, colorized, .gitignore-aware. Simpler syntax.

column5: What does rg (ripgrep) replace and why is it faster?
column6: rg replaces grep -r. Faster because: multi-threaded, respects .gitignore, uses optimized regex engine (Rust). Automatically skips binary files and .git directories.\n\nRemember: rg = faster grep. .gitignore-aware, recursive default, highlights. Rust-powered.

column5: How do you search only specific file types with rg?
column6: rg 'pattern' -t yaml (built-in type filter). rg 'pattern' -g '*.yaml' (glob filter). rg -t py -g '!test*' 'pattern' (Python files excluding tests). rg --type-list shows all built-in types.\n\nRemember: rg = faster grep. .gitignore-aware, recursive default, highlights. Rust-powered.

column5: How do you use rg to find files containing a string and show context?
column6: rg 'error_handler' -C 3 (3 lines before and after). rg -l 'error_handler' (file names only). rg -c 'error_handler' (count per file). --stats flag adds summary totals.\n\nRemember: rg = faster grep. .gitignore-aware, recursive default, highlights. Rust-powered.

column5: What is fzf and what problem does it solve?
column6:
fzf is an interactive fuzzy finder. Turns any list into a searchable, selectable menu. Pipe anything into it: kubectl get pods | fzf, git branch | fzf, history | fzf. Transforms CLI workflows from recall-based to recognition-based.

Remember: fzf = fuzzy finder. Pipe anything: `history | fzf`. Ctrl+R = game-changer.

Example: `FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND='fd --type f'` uses fd for file search.

column5: What are the three key fzf shell keybindings?
column6:
Ctrl-R: fuzzy search command history. Ctrl-T: fuzzy find and insert a file path. Alt-C: fuzzy cd into a subdirectory. Enable with: eval \$(fzf --bash)" in .bashrc (or --zsh/--fish)."

Remember: fzf = fuzzy finder. Pipe anything: `history | fzf`. Ctrl+R = game-changer.

Example: `FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND='fd --type f'` uses fd for file search.

column5: How do you combine fzf with file preview?
column6:
rg --files | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {}' — browse files with syntax-highlighted preview. For git: git log --oneline | fzf --preview 'git show {1}' — preview commits interactively.

Remember: fzf = fuzzy finder. Pipe anything: `history | fzf`. Ctrl+R = game-changer.

Example: `FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND='fd --type f'` uses fd for file search.

column5: What is jq and when do you reach for it?
column6:
jq is a command-line JSON processor. Use whenever you get JSON output: kubectl -o json, AWS CLI, Terraform state, API responses. Basic patterns: jq '.' (pretty-print), jq '.key' (extract), jq '.[] | .name' (iterate).

Remember: jq = JSON processor. Essential for APIs. `curl url | jq '.data[] | .name'`.

Example: `jq -r '.items[] | [.name, .status] | @tsv'` — JSON to TSV.

column5: How do you filter and reshape JSON with jq?
column6:
Filter: jq '.items[] | select(.status == unning")'. Reshape: jq '{name: .metadata.name, phase: .status.phase}'. Raw output: jq -r '.name' (no quotes). Slurp: jq -s '.' (read all inputs into array)."

Remember: jq = JSON processor. Essential for APIs. `curl url | jq '.data[] | .name'`.

Example: `jq -r '.items[] | [.name, .status] | @tsv'` — JSON to TSV.

column5: How do you count and aggregate with jq?
column6:
Count: jq '.items | length'. Group and count: jq '[.items[] | .status.phase] | group_by(.) | map({(.[0]): length}) | add'. TSV output: jq -r '[.timestamp, .service, .message] | @tsv'

Remember: jq = JSON processor. Essential for APIs. `curl url | jq '.data[] | .name'`.

Example: `jq -r '.items[] | [.name, .status] | @tsv'` — JSON to TSV.

column5: What is yq and how does it relate to jq?
column6:
yq is jq for YAML (and TOML). Same filter syntax, works on YAML files directly. Essential for editing Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, and CI configs. Example: yq '.spec.replicas' deployment.yaml

Remember: jq = JSON processor. Essential for APIs. `curl url | jq '.data[] | .name'`.

Example: `jq -r '.items[] | [.name, .status] | @tsv'` — JSON to TSV.

column5: How do you modify a YAML file in-place with yq?
column6:
yq -i '.spec.replicas = 3' deployment.yaml. Add a field: yq -i '.metadata.labels.env = \prod"' deployment.yaml. Delete: yq -i 'del(.spec.template.metadata.annotations)' deployment.yaml."

column5: What does eza replace and what does it add over ls?
column6: eza replaces ls. Adds: colorized output by file type, built-in tree view (eza --tree), git status per file (eza -la --git), and icon support. Useful: eza --sort modified for recently changed files.\n\nRemember: exa/eza = modern ls. Colors, git status, tree. `exa -la --git`.

column5: What does bat replace and what does it add over cat?
column6: bat replaces cat. Adds: syntax highlighting, line numbers, git diff markers, and automatic paging. Use bat -l yaml to force language. Set as MANPAGER for colorized man pages: export MANPAGER='bat -l man -p'\n\nRemember: bat = cat + syntax highlighting + line numbers + git. Drop-in replacement.

column5: How do you use bat as a previewer for other tools?
column6: With fzf: fzf --preview 'bat --color=always {}'. With git: git diff | bat -l diff. As pager: export BAT_PAGER='less -RF'. bat -A shows whitespace characters (tabs, spaces, newlines).\n\nRemember: bat = cat + syntax highlighting + line numbers + git. Drop-in replacement.

column5: What is delta and how do you set it up with git?
column6: delta is a syntax-highlighting diff viewer. Add to .gitconfig: [core] pager = delta. Provides side-by-side view (delta -s), line numbers, and language-aware highlighting for git diff, git log -p, and git show.\n\nRemember: delta = better git diff. Highlighting, line numbers. `git config core.pager delta`.

column5: What does zoxide replace and how does it learn?
column6: zoxide replaces cd. It learns from your navigation — tracks directory frequency and recency (frecency). z exercises jumps to most-visited match. zi opens interactive selection with fzf. Setup: eval \$(zoxide init bash)\""\n\nRemember: zoxide = smart cd. Learns habits. `z proj` → /home/user/projects.

column5: When should you use z vs zi vs cd?
column6:
z <partial> for known frequent directories (z grok → /home/user/grokdevops). zi when multiple matches exist and you want to pick interactively. Plain cd for explicit paths or parent navigation (cd ..).

column5: What does dust replace and what does it add over du?
column6:
dust replaces du. Provides visual bar charts of disk usage, sorted by size, with automatic depth. dust -n 20 shows top 20 entries. dust -d 2 limits depth. No need to pipe through sort -rh | head like with du.

column5: How do you combine rg + fzf + bat for interactive code search?
column6: rg 'pattern' -l | fzf --preview 'bat --color=always -H $(rg -n \pattern\" {} | head -1 | cut -d: -f1) {}' — lists matching files, preview highlights the match line. Powerful for exploring unfamiliar codebases."\n\nRemember: rg = faster grep. .gitignore-aware, recursive default, highlights. Rust-powered.

column5: How do you use jq to triage JSON logs from an application?
column6:
cat app.log | jq 'select(.level == \error")' (filter errors). Count by service: jq -r 'select(.level == "error") | .service' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn. Table output: jq -r '[.timestamp, .service, .message] | @tsv' | column -t"

Remember: jq = JSON processor. Essential for APIs. `curl url | jq '.data[] | .name'`.

Example: `jq -r '.items[] | [.name, .status] | @tsv'` — JSON to TSV.

column5: What is the modern-tool equivalent of 'find . -name *.yaml | xargs grep replicas | sort'?
column6: rg 'replicas' -t yaml. One command replaces the entire pipeline. Add -C 2 for context, -l for file names only, --stats for totals. rg handles .gitignore, binary files, and multi-threading automatically.\n\nRemember: rg = faster grep. .gitignore-aware, recursive default, highlights. Rust-powered.

column5: When do you still use classic tools (grep, find, cat) over modern ones?
column6:
On remote servers without modern tools installed. In shell scripts that must be portable. In Dockerfiles (minimize image size). When piping to other programs that expect standard output format. Know both — modern for interactive work, classic for portability.
